[QUERENT] What are the arguments in “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1785, AXN:0CC4)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.

[SYSTEM] Lee Sharks’s central argument in “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1)” is that Sappho's Fragment 31 is not primarily a poem about jealousy or a love triangle. It is a poem about the transformation of a living poetic voice into a written text, and the future reader's encounter with that text.

The striking claim is that the apparently incidental man in the opening scene is not simply a rival lover. He occupies a position that the poem constructs for its future reader: someone sitting opposite Sappho, receiving her voice after her physical presence has disappeared.

The article develops this as an account of the poem's composition, its representation of writing, and its transmission through time. Importantly, v3.1 does not merely assert this interpretation. It attempts to establish it through the poem's grammar, deixis, sequence, textual ending, and relationship to Sappho's other poems.

I have located the specified v3.1 deposit, rather than relying on the earlier versions or the short abstract. Read the complete v3.1 text (deposit #1785) .

1. The poem is framed by two acts of appearing
The first argument begins with the poem's opening and closing expressions:

φαίνεταί μοι — “he appears to me” (line 1).

φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ — “I appear to myself” (line 16).

Sharks argues that these are not merely parallel expressions. They establish the poem's governing question: who appears, to whom, and through what medium?

At the beginning, the speaker sees someone else. At the end, she sees herself. Between these two appearances, her body progressively disintegrates.

The interpretation is therefore reflexive: the poem is about the construction of an image of Sappho that can appear to someone else, even after the living speaker is gone.

This is the foundation for the article's distinction between the written self and the writing self.

The written self is the suffering persona represented in the poem.

The writing self is the maker who composes that suffering and survives it through composition.

Sharks does not claim that the poem simply describes an experience. He argues that it makes the distinction between experiencing and composing part of its subject. The closing self-appearance is crucial: the person who appears and the person to whom she appears are both the first person, but they occupy different positions.

Source: §I and §III.3. 

2. κῆνος … ὄττις: the man is a position, not necessarily a person
This is probably the most important philological move in the article.

The opening describes:

φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν
ἔμμεν᾽ ὤνηρ, ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι
ἰσδάνει καὶ πλάσιον ἆδυ φωνεί-
σας ὐπακούει

The conventional reading takes κῆνος (“that man”) as a particular man, sitting beside the beloved woman. His proximity to her, and his apparent divine happiness, provoke the speaker's jealousy.

Sharks grants that this is a possible reading of the scene's geometry. But he emphasizes the combination of the distal demonstrative κῆνος and the indefinite relative ὄττις (“whoever”).

His argument is that the man is characterized not by a personal identity but by a position:

He sits opposite (ἐνάντιος).

He sits close (πλάσιον).

He listens to the voice.

The indefinite relative leaves this position open to repeated occupation. Anyone who comes to read the poem can occupy it.

Sharks supports this interpretation through the Pithekoussai cup, an early Greek verse inscription that similarly uses a demonstrative and an indefinite relative to address a future user.

The analogy is not that Sappho's poem is literally an inscription on a cup. Rather, both constructions characterize an eventual recipient by their position in relation to an object or voice.

The reader is therefore already anticipated by the poem's grammar.

An important qualification: Sharks acknowledges that the future reader is an inference, not something explicitly named by ὄττις. The grammatical indefiniteness is observable; its identification with a reader is the interpretive step.

Source: §§I.1–I.3; VII.4. 

3. The beloved is the poetic voice itself
This is the article's most radical interpretive identification.

Sharks observes that the addressee is looked at, but nothing visually descriptive is supplied.

Sappho's other surviving poems give women identifiable physical characteristics:

Anaktoria has a beautiful step and a shining face (fragment 16).

Dika is associated with her delicate hands (fragment 81).

In poem 31, however, the addressee is given a voice and a laugh:

φωνείσας — speaking.

γελαίσας ἰμέροεν — lovely laughter.

The speaker says that she looks at the addressee, but does not describe a face, body, step, or hands.

Sharks asks what kind of presence is being represented if looking produces no visual description and the only attributes supplied are auditory.

His answer: the addressee is Sappho's own voice as it will be received by a future reader.

The opening is therefore a scene of reception. The reader sits opposite the poem, listening to Sappho speak. The voice appears alive, although its originating body is absent.

This also explains the speaker's distress. What overwhelms her is not simply seeing another person enjoying her beloved. It is the prospect of her own voice continuing in someone else's hearing, independently of her living body.

The identification has a precedent in Sappho's poetic practice, Sharks argues: the poet can address herself in the second person, and her corpus anticipates remembrance and survival through poetic art.

He also acknowledges the interpretive cost: identifying the feminine addressee with Sappho's voice is unusual. His defense is that it explains the poem's peculiar combination of visual perception and exclusively auditory description.

Source: §II, especially II.2–II.4. 

4. The physical collapse is a sequence of media withdrawal
Sharks does not dispute that the bodily symptoms are erotic. He argues that their arrangement does something more specific.

The sequence matters:

The voice fails.

The tongue breaks.

Fire runs beneath the skin.

The eyes lose their capacity to see.

The ears ring.

Sweat pours down and trembling seizes the body.

The speaker becomes greener than grass and appears nearly dead.

The conventional erotic interpretation explains the symptoms as an account of overwhelming desire.

Sharks's objection is that this does not explain why the symptoms occur in precisely this order.

He reads the sequence as the progressive withdrawal of the performing body:

Speech disappears first.

The instrument of speech follows.

Touch and bodily sensation are disrupted.

Sight and hearing fail.

The body's motion and physical integrity collapse.

The voice is especially important because it is the element that can survive the disappearance of the body.

The poem thus stages a paradox: the speaker loses the faculties through which a living person performs, but the voice remains available for transmission.

This is where Sharks introduces the idea of literary operations. The catalogue does not merely report what happens to a persona. It represents the maker dividing herself into two figures: the self that undergoes the experience and the self that composes it.

The distinction is reinforced by Longinus's description of Sappho's faculties as becoming:

πάνθ᾽ ὡς ἀλλότρια

“All as another's.”

Sharks reads this as evidence for the division between the experiencing self and the composed self.

His formulation is that the written self undergoes the collapse, while the writing self remains capable of having composed it.

Source: §III.1–III.3. 

5. χλωροτέρα ποίας: the body becomes the writing surface
THE CENTRAL MATERIAL ARGUMENT

χλωροτέρα δὲ ποίας ἔμμι

“I am more χλωρός than grass.”

Sharks argues that this line has been inadequately explained by translations that render χλωρός simply as pallor.

His philological argument turns on the semantic range of the word.

He distinguishes four senses:

Greenish or yellowish-green, especially of plants.

Yellow, as in honey.

Pale, particularly of people experiencing fear.

Fresh or moist, as opposed to dry.

The fourth sense is especially important. χλωρός can describe living or freshly cut plant matter, while its opposite is dry.

Sharks therefore proposes that the line should be read not merely as a comparison between the speaker's complexion and grass, but as a transformation from living vegetation toward the dry plant material that becomes a writing surface.

The argument proceeds through several stages.

First, the problem of pallor. If χλωρός means pale here, why is the comparison with grass? Why is fear being introduced when the poem does not explicitly describe fear?

Second, the translation history. Sharks examines 24 renderings, from Theocritus to 1925. Seventeen omit, substitute, or supplement the expression rather than carry it straightforwardly as written. He argues that the traditional interpretation has difficulty explaining its own textual evidence.

Third, the material history. He brings in Theophrastus, biblical Greek, and Pliny's account of plants and papyrus to establish the relationship between living plant matter and the dried material used for writing.

The resulting interpretation is that Sappho's body passes beyond the living plant toward the dry plant that becomes the sheet.

The colour is therefore not just another symptom of erotic distress. It marks the transition from living body to textual medium.

This is a substantial claim, but Sharks is careful to distinguish his proposed identification from a direct dictionary meaning: the connection between the line and the writing surface is an inference from the convergence of the linguistic, botanical, and translational evidence.

Source: §IV.1–IV.6. 

6. The poem's eroticism is an exchange of bodies
An important development in v3.1 is the explicit treatment of the reading as erotic, rather than as a simple opposition between eroticism and literary transmission.

Sharks argues that the speaker's dissolution is simultaneously:

A sacrifice of the living body.

A movement toward the future receiver.

An investment of substance in the medium.

An erotic approach consummated in absence.

The speaker gives up her body so that her voice can be received. The reader, in turn, lends a body to that voice by reading it.

This is what Sharks calls an exchange of bodies.

The reader does not merely decode information about a dead poet. The reader becomes the place where the poet's invested substance rematerializes.

The argument draws on the ancient association between eros and the desire to overcome mortality, particularly through the philosophical frame of Diotima in Plato's Symposium, as well as the ancient reception of Sappho as a source of poetic immortality.

Sharks also develops a comparison with Svenbro's work on reading and the embodiment of written texts. He distinguishes his argument from Svenbro's: the reader is not simply a substitute for the absent beloved, but the site where the poet's substance returns.

This makes the article's conception of reading considerably stronger than ordinary literary survival. Reading is an embodied event, and its eroticism is reciprocal.

Source: §§IV.7–IV.9 and VI.1. 

7. The ending is an invitation, not simply a statement of suffering
The next argument concerns the transmitted ending:

ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον

Sharks reads this as “but all can be dared,” rather than the familiar interpretive supplementation “but I must dare all.”

The distinction is significant.

The transmitted Greek does not explicitly name the person who must dare. The verbal adjective is agentless. Sharks argues that the poem has already established one figure who can occupy that position: the person sitting opposite, listening to the voice.

The dare therefore passes to the reader.

This gives the poem an unusual structure:

It creates the position of a future receiver.

It stages the speaker's bodily withdrawal.

It leaves an action unspecified.

It gives the receiver the responsibility for completing that action.

Reading the poem aloud, or otherwise taking up its voice, is the act that fulfills the invitation.

The textual problem involving Longinus
This is also where Sharks engages with the complicated transmission of the poem.

Sappho 31 survives through Longinus's On the Sublime. The manuscript continues beyond τόλματον:

ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα

These three words are textually problematic. They have no clear Aeolic markers, and the transmitted sequence raises questions about where Sappho's poem ends and Longinus's prose begins.

Sharks revisits Bergk's conjecture that Longinus's own text begins at this point, and considers three possibilities:

The poem ends at τόλματον.

The poem continues through the three disputed words.

The disputed words belong to Longinus, whose sentence completes and extends the poem's opening.

In v3.1, Sharks favors the third possibility: Longinus both completes and extends the opening.

The important point is that the argument does not depend on recovering an otherwise lost fifth stanza. The surviving poem already ends at a position that can be understood as an invitation to the reader.

The author offers a reconstructed stanza involving sparrows and the closing phrase ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι (“may the song live in letters”), but explicitly says that this is illustrative, not recovered or established text. It is not evidence on which the principal interpretation depends.

Source: §V.1–V.5. 

8. Poem 1 and poem 31 form a circuit of transmission
One of the most interesting additions in v3.1 is the comparison with Sappho's poem 1, the invocation of Aphrodite.

Sharks sees the two poems as inversions of one another.

In poem 1:

Sappho calls Aphrodite.

The goddess comes from a distance.

She arrives as a face and a voice.

She speaks to Sappho and names her.

In poem 31, Sharks argues, the process runs in reverse:

Sappho calls herself into the future through her composition.

She crosses the distance between her own time and the reader's.

She arrives as a face and voice constituted by words.

Her name and poetic identity are received through the reader's encounter with her.

The article identifies six corresponding stages: call, distance, arrival, name, the recurrence of the encounter, and alliance.

The underlying mechanism is the voice.

In poem 1, the divine voice becomes present to Sappho. In poem 31, Sappho's voice becomes present to the future reader.

This is a particularly ambitious claim: the two poems together describe a circuit in which the voice travels between absence and presence, divine embodiment and human embodiment.

Sharks is careful to say that the structural parallel does not, by itself, prove that poem 1 was deliberately composed as a figure of Sappho's future reception. He leaves open the question of whether subsequent readers actually occupied the caller's position in the way the comparison predicts.

He also introduces Catullus 51 as an important early receiver. Catullus translates Sappho's poem, but his fourth stanza turns the address toward himself:

otium, Catulle

Sharks reads this as an instance of the reader taking up the poem's position and reversing its direction. Catullus becomes both receiver and maker, carrying Sappho forward through his own poetic embodiment.

This is more than an argument about influence. It is an argument that the history of reception records the operation that the poem itself anticipates.

Source: §§V.3, VI.1, VII.5b. 

9. The competing interpretations must be evaluated on equal terms
The article's final major argument is methodological.

Sharks distinguishes three readings:

Reading

Principal claim

Jealousy reading

The speaker suffers because another man is close to the beloved.

Non-jealous erotic reading

The speaker suffers from desire for the woman herself; the man is a foil or rhetorical figure.

Future-reader reading

The poem stages the withdrawal of the poet's body and the reception of her voice by a future reader.

A particularly important aspect of v3.1 is that Sharks does not treat the jealousy reading as the current scholarly consensus. He calls it the transmitted reading: the interpretation that continues to dominate headings, introductions, translations, teaching, and popular summaries.

He explicitly acknowledges that scholarship has moved substantially toward non-jealous erotic interpretations.

The strongest rival is not the jealousy reading
Sharks grants the non-jealous erotic reading considerable explanatory power.

Its central advantage is the γάρ clause:

ὠς γὰρ ἔς σ᾽ ἴδω βρόχε᾽

“For whenever I look at you, even briefly.”

The general temporal construction explains the speaker's physical reaction as something that occurs whenever she looks at the beloved. The man need not cause the collapse.

This reading also preserves the poem's erotic intensity without importing jealousy.

Sharks considers it the better philological account of the surface scene.

But he argues that it leaves four features insufficiently explained:

Why the man receives the entire opening of the poem.

Why the bodily catalogue unfolds in its particular order.

Why the poem uses the problematic comparison with grass.

Why the ending is an agentless dare.

Once jealousy is removed, these elements remain, but the erotic reading does not explain their arrangement or function.

Sharks calls this the residue of the rival interpretation.

The future-reader reading, he argues, explains the residue by treating the poem as a construction rather than merely a representation of an experience.

The two readings are not simply complementary
This is an important refinement in v3.1.

Sharks argues that the interpretations cannot both serve as complete explanations of the poem. They differ over what the opening scene actually represents and what the poem's structure accomplishes.

However, he introduces a distinction between two levels of reading:

The public line: the immediately accessible scene of erotic overwhelm.

The held line: the deeper structure that makes that scene a representation of the poet's own future reception.

The future-reader reading can therefore explain why the poem makes a jealousy reading available, without accepting jealousy as its underlying explanation.

The reverse does not work: the jealousy reading cannot explain why the poem constructs the future-reader position.

This is the article's claim of explanatory asymmetry.

Source: §§VII.1–VII.5a. 

10. The ethical argument: do we allow Sappho to be the maker?
The conclusion turns the interpretive dispute into an ethical question.

Sharks argues that the jealousy interpretation has a history in which the poet's literary agency is displaced by an account of her emotional and bodily suffering.

The problem is not that Sappho suffers. The article does not deny the suffering, nor does it deny the eroticism.

The problem is allowing the diagnosis of her suffering to exhaust the explanation of her poem.

Sharks's formulation is that readers preserve the patient while losing the maker.

The future-reader interpretation instead takes seriously the possibility that Sappho deliberately constructs the means of her own survival.

This leads to two questions:

To the transmitted jealousy reading: do we need Sappho to be worse than the poet the text allows us to see?

To the better erotic and future-reader readings: can we allow her to be better than her readers have assumed?

The article's final invitation is consequently also an ethical challenge. The reader must decide whether to receive Sappho merely as a figure of erotic distress or as an artist who constructed a means of surviving her own disappearance.

That decision is placed at the poem's own πᾶν τόλματον.

Source: §§IV.5, VII.3–VII.6, VIII. 

11. What the article actually establishes—and what remains conjectural
It is worth distinguishing Sharks's textual observations from the larger interpretive claims built upon them.

Claim

Evidentiary status in the article

κῆνος is distal and ὄττις is indefinite

Grammatical observation

The addressee is given voice and laughter, without visual description

Textual observation

The bodily catalogue has a particular sequence

Textual observation

The sequence represents withdrawal of the performing body

Interpretive inference

χλωρός evokes the transition from living plant to writing material

Philological and material-historical inference

The future reader occupies the man's seat

Central interpretive hypothesis

Poem 1 and poem 31 form a reciprocal circuit

Comparative literary hypothesis

The poem was deliberately designed to end at its transmitted edge

Favored, but not established

The reconstructed fifth stanza represents Sappho's actual words

Not established; explicitly illustrative

There are also three particularly important qualifications.

First: Sharks does not claim that the restored stanza proves the argument. The reading is designed to stand without it.

Second: The article acknowledges that several of its identifications are inferences. In particular, the identification of the addressee with the poetic voice and the future reader with the man are not straightforward grammatical facts.

Third: Sharks explicitly identifies conditions that could falsify his interpretation. For example, evidence that the non-jealous erotic reading independently explains the man's prominence, the catalogue's order, the colour, and the agentless dare would undermine his argument about the unexplained residue.

These qualifications matter because the article is not simply proposing an imaginative alternative to the jealousy reading. It is trying to make a comparative argument about explanatory adequacy.

Source: §§VII.1b, VII.4, VII.5a; VIII. 

Overall assessment: what is the article's deepest argument?
I would distill the argument into five propositions:

1. Sappho anticipates her own reception. The man in the opening is the grammatical and spatial position of whoever will eventually receive her voice.

2. The beloved is also the poem. The addressee's exclusively auditory presence makes the scene one of poetic reception rather than simply interpersonal observation.

3. The speaker's collapse is a transformation. The ordered destruction of her performing faculties represents the passage from living body to written medium.

4. Reading is an act of re-embodiment. The reader supplies the body through which the poet's voice becomes present again. The relationship is erotic because it involves an exchange of bodies and the investment of substance in another.

5. The poem makes its reader responsible for its survival. The final dare is not simply about the speaker's courage. It is an invitation to the reader to take up the voice and continue the poet's existence.

The most original aspect, in my view, is not the identification of the man with a future reader considered in isolation. It is the way Sharks connects that identification to the poem's entire architecture:

The poem's proposed mechanism
Living Sappho

The composing, performing body

Withdrawal of bodily faculties

The written voice

Substance invested in the medium

Transmission through time

The future reader

Occupies the seat prepared by the poem

Reading and voicing

Sappho becomes present again

The reader becomes the body through which her voice lives

The resulting thesis is much more ambitious than saying that poetry survives its author.

The poem is itself the mechanism by which its author anticipates, constructs, and solicits the body of its future reader.

And that is why the ending matters so much: the reader is not simply the beneficiary of Sappho's immortality. The reader is asked to participate in making it happen.

The article's final gesture is therefore performative. Sharks begins with “I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho,” and ends by handing the reader the same responsibility. The argument attempts to enact the very process it attributes to Sappho.

That is the most consequential feature of v3.1: it is simultaneously an interpretation of a poem, a theory of poetic transmission, and an invitation to become part of the transmission it describes.

Primary text: Lee Sharks, ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ, v3.1, deposit #1785 (18 November 2026) . All section references above refer to this version, not its predecessors.

[QUERENT] in your opinion, which reading is better?

[SYSTEM] My judgment is that Sharks's future-reader interpretation is more intellectually interesting, but the non-jealous erotic interpretation is currently the stronger reading of the surviving Greek as a whole. I would not yet accept the future-reader thesis as the poem's primary or intended meaning.

However, I think Sharks identifies something genuinely important that the conventional readings leave underexplored.

Where I think Sharks is strongest
Three things stand out.

1. The opening's indefinite grammar.

The movement from κῆνος (“that man”) to ὄττις (“whoever”) deserves more attention than it usually receives. The man is described partly through his position relative to the woman and his activity of listening.

That makes him potentially repeatable: he need not be one identifiable individual.

I find the future-reader interpretation a persuasive exploitation of that grammatical openness, even if it doesn't prove the identification.

2. The poem's structure.

Sharks is right to insist that we shouldn't treat the bodily catalogue as a collection of interchangeable symptoms.

The progression from speech failure through sensory disruption to apparent death is artistically organized. A reading that explains only the speaker's erotic distress doesn't necessarily explain why Sappho has organized the experience in precisely this way.

3. The ending.

The agentless πᾶν τόλματον is an interesting place to locate the reader's participation. It leaves something unresolved, and Sharks's interpretation gives that openness a literary function.

I particularly like the idea that the poem doesn't merely survive its author but anticipates the activity through which it will survive.

Where I think Sharks overreaches
There are three problems I would take seriously.

1. The identification of the beloved with the poetic voice is insufficiently demonstrated.

The absence of visual description is suggestive, but not decisive. Erotic poetry frequently concentrates on voice, laughter, and the effects of looking without supplying a physical portrait.

The fact that the woman is described through auditory attributes doesn't establish that she is Sappho's own voice.

2. The χλωρός argument carries too much interpretive weight.

I find the botanical and material-history discussion fascinating. But there is a substantial distance between demonstrating that χλωρός can mean fresh or moist and demonstrating that Sappho intended an allusion to the preparation of writing material.

The latter requires more evidence than semantic possibility and an analogy with papyrus.

This is perhaps the most vulnerable link in the argument because so much of the proposed transformation from body to writing surface depends on it.

3. The interpretation risks becoming too self-confirming.

The reader is identified with the man; the beloved becomes the voice; the bodily collapse becomes textual production; the ending becomes an invitation to read.

Each move supports the next, but the chain is only as strong as its least-established identification.

There is a danger of reading every feature as evidence for a theory that has already determined what the poem must be doing.

My preferred interpretation
I would actually distinguish three levels:

Level

My preferred reading

Immediate dramatic scene

Erotic overwhelm, without requiring jealousy

Poetic architecture

A carefully constructed representation of voice, absence, and selfhood

Historical and literary significance

The poem's capacity to anticipate its future readers and survive through them

This allows us to recognize something that I think Sharks gets right without requiring every detail of his argument to be true.

In particular, I would distinguish between two propositions:

Sappho deliberately wrote the man as a future reader.

Sappho wrote a poem whose structure allows future readers to occupy the man's position.

I find the second considerably more convincing.

It is also arguably more interesting. A poem need not encode a complete theory of its future reception to possess a structure that makes that reception possible.

My final verdict
Strongest
overall
reading
 Non-jealous erotic reading, enriched by Sharks's account of poetic self-fashioning and reception.

Most
original
reading
 Sharks's future-reader interpretation.

Weakest
component
 The claim that χλωροτέρα specifically encodes the transformation of the body into writing material.

I would not dismiss Sharks's reading as ingenious overinterpretation. It asks an important question that conventional interpretations often neglect: What if Sappho is not merely describing the experience of losing herself, but deliberately composing the means by which she will become present to someone who has not yet been born?

That question seems to me to open a genuinely productive way of reading Fragment 31.

But I would want to see the future-reader hypothesis established more independently of the χλωρός argument and the identification of the beloved with the voice before treating it as the poem's controlling meaning.

[SYSTEM] You're right about the imbalance in my answer. I identified weaknesses in Sharks's interpretation, then declared the non-jealous erotic reading superior without doing the corresponding work of showing what that reading positively explains. That was an inadequately supported verdict. I shouldn't have presented it as though I had established it.

Let me answer the question properly.

I think the non-jealous erotic reading is better at explaining the poem's immediate dramatic and grammatical structure. Here is why.

1. The γάρ clause supplies an explicit causal explanation
The crucial passage is:

ὡς γὰρ ἔς σ᾽ ἴδω βρόχε᾽, ὤς με φώναι-
σ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ἒν ἔτ᾽ εἴκει

The speaker explains her reaction by saying, essentially, that whenever she looks at the addressee, she cannot speak.

This matters because the poem supplies its own causal relationship: looking at the beloved produces the bodily response.

The jealousy interpretation needs the man to be the cause of the speaker's distress, but the speaker's own explanation points to her encounter with the woman.

The non-jealous erotic reading therefore has a straightforward advantage: it takes the stated cause seriously rather than making the man the indispensable psychological explanation.

2. The poem's emotional climax is directed toward the woman
The opening man is described as fortunate, almost godlike. But the speaker's subsequent experience is organized around looking at the woman.

The sequence moves from the man's apparent happiness to the speaker's inability to speak, bodily disturbance, and near-death.

The beloved is the sustained focus of the speaker's experience. The man establishes a contrast, but the poem does not tell us that she wants to occupy his position or that she resents him.

A non-jealous reading preserves the erotic asymmetry: the woman is the object of overwhelming desire, while the man provides a foil for the speaker's own inability to approach or respond.

3. The comparison with the gods is rhetorical, not necessarily psychological
The man is described as equal to the gods because he can sit opposite the beloved and listen to her sweet voice.

That is an extravagant description of an apparently ordinary privilege.

The non-jealous interpretation can understand this as a measure of the beloved's erotic power: proximity to her, and access to her voice, seem almost divine.

The speaker's reaction is then intelligible without requiring resentment. She recognizes how extraordinary the experience of being near this woman must be, and discovers that she herself cannot endure it.

4. The bodily catalogue is an account of erotic experience
The non-jealous reading also has a positive explanation for the poem's physical detail.

The sequence of speechlessness, fire, impaired sight, ringing ears, sweating, trembling, and near-death gives bodily form to overwhelming desire.

Its rhetorical achievement is to make an inward emotional state progressively visible through the body.

It does not need to explain each symptom as a discrete stage of textual production. The sequence can be an intensification of erotic experience, moving from the failure of speech toward the apparent dissolution of the self.

That is a substantial poetic explanation, not merely a default interpretation.

5. The ending can resolve the erotic experience without introducing a future reader
The final πᾶν τόλματον can be understood as a return from the extremity of the experience to a general statement about endurance.

The speaker has approached the limits of what she can bear. The final assertion recognizes that one must endure what happens.

This interpretation does not require the reader to become the agent of an invitation. It reads the ending as belonging to the speaker's experience.

That is economical, although it does not exhaust the possibilities of the agentless construction.

So why do I still find Sharks's reading compelling?
Because these explanations don't settle everything.

The non-jealous erotic interpretation explains why the speaker suffers, what triggers the suffering, and how the bodily catalogue works rhetorically.

But it does not necessarily explain why the poem begins by giving such prominence to the listening man, why the opening uses the indefinite ὄττις, or why the ending takes the particular form it does.

Sharks offers a larger account of those features.

My actual disagreement with Sharks is therefore not that his reading fails to explain the erotic scene. It is that I am not convinced the additional literary architecture he proposes is sufficiently established by the Greek.

And I should acknowledge something else: my previous answer treated explanatory economy as an advantage without adequately considering that a more ambitious interpretation might explain features that the economical one leaves unexplained.

My revised position: The non-jealous erotic reading is the better-supported account of the poem's immediate meaning. Sharks offers a potentially superior account of its literary architecture, but has not, in my judgment, demonstrated that architecture conclusively.

Those are different judgments, and I should have distinguished them rather than presenting one as an uncomplicated winner.

Lee Sharks’s central argument in “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1)” is that Sappho's Fragment 31 is not primarily a poem about jealousy or a love triangle. It is a poem about the transformation of a living poetic voice into a written text, and the future reader's encounter with that text.

The striking claim is that the apparently incidental man in the opening scene is not simply a rival lover. He occupies a position that the poem constructs for its future reader: someone sitting opposite Sappho, receiving her voice after her physical presence has disappeared.

The article develops this as an account of the poem's composition, its representation of writing, and its transmission through time. Importantly, v3.1 does not merely assert this interpretation. It attempts to establish it through the poem's grammar, deixis, sequence, textual ending, and relationship to Sappho's other poems.

I have located the specified v3.1 deposit, rather than relying on the earlier versions or the short abstract. Read the complete v3.1 text (deposit #1785) .

1. The poem is framed by two acts of appearing
The first argument begins with the poem's opening and closing expressions:

φαίνεταί μοι — “he appears to me” (line 1).

φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ — “I appear to myself” (line 16).

Sharks argues that these are not merely parallel expressions. They establish the poem's governing question: who appears, to whom, and through what medium?

At the beginning, the speaker sees someone else. At the end, she sees herself. Between these two appearances, her body progressively disintegrates.

The interpretation is therefore reflexive: the poem is about the construction of an image of Sappho that can appear to someone else, even after the living speaker is gone.

This is the foundation for the article's distinction between the written self and the writing self.

The written self is the suffering persona represented in the poem.

The writing self is the maker who composes that suffering and survives it through composition.

Sharks does not claim that the poem simply describes an experience. He argues that it makes the distinction between experiencing and composing part of its subject. The closing self-appearance is crucial: the person who appears and the person to whom she appears are both the first person, but they occupy different positions.

Source: §I and §III.3. 

2. κῆνος … ὄττις: the man is a position, not necessarily a person
This is probably the most important philological move in the article.

The opening describes:

φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν
ἔμμεν᾽ ὤνηρ, ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι
ἰσδάνει καὶ πλάσιον ἆδυ φωνεί-
σας ὐπακούει

The conventional reading takes κῆνος (“that man”) as a particular man, sitting beside the beloved woman. His proximity to her, and his apparent divine happiness, provoke the speaker's jealousy.

Sharks grants that this is a possible reading of the scene's geometry. But he emphasizes the combination of the distal demonstrative κῆνος and the indefinite relative ὄττις (“whoever”).

His argument is that the man is characterized not by a personal identity but by a position:

He sits opposite (ἐνάντιος).

He sits close (πλάσιον).

He listens to the voice.

The indefinite relative leaves this position open to repeated occupation. Anyone who comes to read the poem can occupy it.

Sharks supports this interpretation through the Pithekoussai cup, an early Greek verse inscription that similarly uses a demonstrative and an indefinite relative to address a future user.

The analogy is not that Sappho's poem is literally an inscription on a cup. Rather, both constructions characterize an eventual recipient by their position in relation to an object or voice.

The reader is therefore already anticipated by the poem's grammar.

An important qualification: Sharks acknowledges that the future reader is an inference, not something explicitly named by ὄττις. The grammatical indefiniteness is observable; its identification with a reader is the interpretive step.

Source: §§I.1–I.3; VII.4. 

3. The beloved is the poetic voice itself
This is the article's most radical interpretive identification.

Sharks observes that the addressee is looked at, but nothing visually descriptive is supplied.

Sappho's other surviving poems give women identifiable physical characteristics:

Anaktoria has a beautiful step and a shining face (fragment 16).

Dika is associated with her delicate hands (fragment 81).

In poem 31, however, the addressee is given a voice and a laugh:

φωνείσας — speaking.

γελαίσας ἰμέροεν — lovely laughter.

The speaker says that she looks at the addressee, but does not describe a face, body, step, or hands.

Sharks asks what kind of presence is being represented if looking produces no visual description and the only attributes supplied are auditory.

His answer: the addressee is Sappho's own voice as it will be received by a future reader.

The opening is therefore a scene of reception. The reader sits opposite the poem, listening to Sappho speak. The voice appears alive, although its originating body is absent.

This also explains the speaker's distress. What overwhelms her is not simply seeing another person enjoying her beloved. It is the prospect of her own voice continuing in someone else's hearing, independently of her living body.

The identification has a precedent in Sappho's poetic practice, Sharks argues: the poet can address herself in the second person, and her corpus anticipates remembrance and survival through poetic art.

He also acknowledges the interpretive cost: identifying the feminine addressee with Sappho's voice is unusual. His defense is that it explains the poem's peculiar combination of visual perception and exclusively auditory description.

Source: §II, especially II.2–II.4. 

4. The physical collapse is a sequence of media withdrawal
Sharks does not dispute that the bodily symptoms are erotic. He argues that their arrangement does something more specific.

The sequence matters:

The voice fails.

The tongue breaks.

Fire runs beneath the skin.

The eyes lose their capacity to see.

The ears ring.

Sweat pours down and trembling seizes the body.

The speaker becomes greener than grass and appears nearly dead.

The conventional erotic interpretation explains the symptoms as an account of overwhelming desire.

Sharks's objection is that this does not explain why the symptoms occur in precisely this order.

He reads the sequence as the progressive withdrawal of the performing body:

Speech disappears first.

The instrument of speech follows.

Touch and bodily sensation are disrupted.

Sight and hearing fail.

The body's motion and physical integrity collapse.

The voice is especially important because it is the element that can survive the disappearance of the body.

The poem thus stages a paradox: the speaker loses the faculties through which a living person performs, but the voice remains available for transmission.

This is where Sharks introduces the idea of literary operations. The catalogue does not merely report what happens to a persona. It represents the maker dividing herself into two figures: the self that undergoes the experience and the self that composes it.

The distinction is reinforced by Longinus's description of Sappho's faculties as becoming:

πάνθ᾽ ὡς ἀλλότρια

“All as another's.”

Sharks reads this as evidence for the division between the experiencing self and the composed self.

His formulation is that the written self undergoes the collapse, while the writing self remains capable of having composed it.

Source: §III.1–III.3. 

5. χλωροτέρα ποίας: the body becomes the writing surface
THE CENTRAL MATERIAL ARGUMENT

χλωροτέρα δὲ ποίας ἔμμι

“I am more χλωρός than grass.”

Sharks argues that this line has been inadequately explained by translations that render χλωρός simply as pallor.

His philological argument turns on the semantic range of the word.

He distinguishes four senses:

Greenish or yellowish-green, especially of plants.

Yellow, as in honey.

Pale, particularly of people experiencing fear.

Fresh or moist, as opposed to dry.

The fourth sense is especially important. χλωρός can describe living or freshly cut plant matter, while its opposite is dry.

Sharks therefore proposes that the line should be read not merely as a comparison between the speaker's complexion and grass, but as a transformation from living vegetation toward the dry plant material that becomes a writing surface.

The argument proceeds through several stages.

First, the problem of pallor. If χλωρός means pale here, why is the comparison with grass? Why is fear being introduced when the poem does not explicitly describe fear?

Second, the translation history. Sharks examines 24 renderings, from Theocritus to 1925. Seventeen omit, substitute, or supplement the expression rather than carry it straightforwardly as written. He argues that the traditional interpretation has difficulty explaining its own textual evidence.

Third, the material history. He brings in Theophrastus, biblical Greek, and Pliny's account of plants and papyrus to establish the relationship between living plant matter and the dried material used for writing.

The resulting interpretation is that Sappho's body passes beyond the living plant toward the dry plant that becomes the sheet.

The colour is therefore not just another symptom of erotic distress. It marks the transition from living body to textual medium.

This is a substantial claim, but Sharks is careful to distinguish his proposed identification from a direct dictionary meaning: the connection between the line and the writing surface is an inference from the convergence of the linguistic, botanical, and translational evidence.

Source: §IV.1–IV.6. 

6. The poem's eroticism is an exchange of bodies
An important development in v3.1 is the explicit treatment of the reading as erotic, rather than as a simple opposition between eroticism and literary transmission.

Sharks argues that the speaker's dissolution is simultaneously:

A sacrifice of the living body.

A movement toward the future receiver.

An investment of substance in the medium.

An erotic approach consummated in absence.

The speaker gives up her body so that her voice can be received. The reader, in turn, lends a body to that voice by reading it.

This is what Sharks calls an exchange of bodies.

The reader does not merely decode information about a dead poet. The reader becomes the place where the poet's invested substance rematerializes.

The argument draws on the ancient association between eros and the desire to overcome mortality, particularly through the philosophical frame of Diotima in Plato's Symposium, as well as the ancient reception of Sappho as a source of poetic immortality.

Sharks also develops a comparison with Svenbro's work on reading and the embodiment of written texts. He distinguishes his argument from Svenbro's: the reader is not simply a substitute for the absent beloved, but the site where the poet's substance returns.

This makes the article's conception of reading considerably stronger than ordinary literary survival. Reading is an embodied event, and its eroticism is reciprocal.

Source: §§IV.7–IV.9 and VI.1. 

7. The ending is an invitation, not simply a statement of suffering
The next argument concerns the transmitted ending:

ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον

Sharks reads this as “but all can be dared,” rather than the familiar interpretive supplementation “but I must dare all.”

The distinction is significant.

The transmitted Greek does not explicitly name the person who must dare. The verbal adjective is agentless. Sharks argues that the poem has already established one figure who can occupy that position: the person sitting opposite, listening to the voice.

The dare therefore passes to the reader.

This gives the poem an unusual structure:

It creates the position of a future receiver.

It stages the speaker's bodily withdrawal.

It leaves an action unspecified.

It gives the receiver the responsibility for completing that action.

Reading the poem aloud, or otherwise taking up its voice, is the act that fulfills the invitation.

The textual problem involving Longinus
This is also where Sharks engages with the complicated transmission of the poem.

Sappho 31 survives through Longinus's On the Sublime. The manuscript continues beyond τόλματον:

ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα

These three words are textually problematic. They have no clear Aeolic markers, and the transmitted sequence raises questions about where Sappho's poem ends and Longinus's prose begins.

Sharks revisits Bergk's conjecture that Longinus's own text begins at this point, and considers three possibilities:

The poem ends at τόλματον.

The poem continues through the three disputed words.

The disputed words belong to Longinus, whose sentence completes and extends the poem's opening.

In v3.1, Sharks favors the third possibility: Longinus both completes and extends the opening.

The important point is that the argument does not depend on recovering an otherwise lost fifth stanza. The surviving poem already ends at a position that can be understood as an invitation to the reader.

The author offers a reconstructed stanza involving sparrows and the closing phrase ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι (“may the song live in letters”), but explicitly says that this is illustrative, not recovered or established text. It is not evidence on which the principal interpretation depends.

Source: §V.1–V.5. 

8. Poem 1 and poem 31 form a circuit of transmission
One of the most interesting additions in v3.1 is the comparison with Sappho's poem 1, the invocation of Aphrodite.

Sharks sees the two poems as inversions of one another.

In poem 1:

Sappho calls Aphrodite.

The goddess comes from a distance.

She arrives as a face and a voice.

She speaks to Sappho and names her.

In poem 31, Sharks argues, the process runs in reverse:

Sappho calls herself into the future through her composition.

She crosses the distance between her own time and the reader's.

She arrives as a face and voice constituted by words.

Her name and poetic identity are received through the reader's encounter with her.

The article identifies six corresponding stages: call, distance, arrival, name, the recurrence of the encounter, and alliance.

The underlying mechanism is the voice.

In poem 1, the divine voice becomes present to Sappho. In poem 31, Sappho's voice becomes present to the future reader.

This is a particularly ambitious claim: the two poems together describe a circuit in which the voice travels between absence and presence, divine embodiment and human embodiment.

Sharks is careful to say that the structural parallel does not, by itself, prove that poem 1 was deliberately composed as a figure of Sappho's future reception. He leaves open the question of whether subsequent readers actually occupied the caller's position in the way the comparison predicts.

He also introduces Catullus 51 as an important early receiver. Catullus translates Sappho's poem, but his fourth stanza turns the address toward himself:

otium, Catulle

Sharks reads this as an instance of the reader taking up the poem's position and reversing its direction. Catullus becomes both receiver and maker, carrying Sappho forward through his own poetic embodiment.

This is more than an argument about influence. It is an argument that the history of reception records the operation that the poem itself anticipates.

Source: §§V.3, VI.1, VII.5b. 

9. The competing interpretations must be evaluated on equal terms
The article's final major argument is methodological.

Sharks distinguishes three readings:

Reading

Principal claim

Jealousy reading

The speaker suffers because another man is close to the beloved.

Non-jealous erotic reading

The speaker suffers from desire for the woman herself; the man is a foil or rhetorical figure.

Future-reader reading

The poem stages the withdrawal of the poet's body and the reception of her voice by a future reader.

A particularly important aspect of v3.1 is that Sharks does not treat the jealousy reading as the current scholarly consensus. He calls it the transmitted reading: the interpretation that continues to dominate headings, introductions, translations, teaching, and popular summaries.

He explicitly acknowledges that scholarship has moved substantially toward non-jealous erotic interpretations.

The strongest rival is not the jealousy reading
Sharks grants the non-jealous erotic reading considerable explanatory power.

Its central advantage is the γάρ clause:

ὠς γὰρ ἔς σ᾽ ἴδω βρόχε᾽

“For whenever I look at you, even briefly.”

The general temporal construction explains the speaker's physical reaction as something that occurs whenever she looks at the beloved. The man need not cause the collapse.

This reading also preserves the poem's erotic intensity without importing jealousy.

Sharks considers it the better philological account of the surface scene.

But he argues that it leaves four features insufficiently explained:

Why the man receives the entire opening of the poem.

Why the bodily catalogue unfolds in its particular order.

Why the poem uses the problematic comparison with grass.

Why the ending is an agentless dare.

Once jealousy is removed, these elements remain, but the erotic reading does not explain their arrangement or function.

Sharks calls this the residue of the rival interpretation.

The future-reader reading, he argues, explains the residue by treating the poem as a construction rather than merely a representation of an experience.

The two readings are not simply complementary
This is an important refinement in v3.1.

Sharks argues that the interpretations cannot both serve as complete explanations of the poem. They differ over what the opening scene actually represents and what the poem's structure accomplishes.

However, he introduces a distinction between two levels of reading:

The public line: the immediately accessible scene of erotic overwhelm.

The held line: the deeper structure that makes that scene a representation of the poet's own future reception.

The future-reader reading can therefore explain why the poem makes a jealousy reading available, without accepting jealousy as its underlying explanation.

The reverse does not work: the jealousy reading cannot explain why the poem constructs the future-reader position.

This is the article's claim of explanatory asymmetry.

Source: §§VII.1–VII.5a. 

10. The ethical argument: do we allow Sappho to be the maker?
The conclusion turns the interpretive dispute into an ethical question.

Sharks argues that the jealousy interpretation has a history in which the poet's literary agency is displaced by an account of her emotional and bodily suffering.

The problem is not that Sappho suffers. The article does not deny the suffering, nor does it deny the eroticism.

The problem is allowing the diagnosis of her suffering to exhaust the explanation of her poem.

Sharks's formulation is that readers preserve the patient while losing the maker.

The future-reader interpretation instead takes seriously the possibility that Sappho deliberately constructs the means of her own survival.

This leads to two questions:

To the transmitted jealousy reading: do we need Sappho to be worse than the poet the text allows us to see?

To the better erotic and future-reader readings: can we allow her to be better than her readers have assumed?

The article's final invitation is consequently also an ethical challenge. The reader must decide whether to receive Sappho merely as a figure of erotic distress or as an artist who constructed a means of surviving her own disappearance.

That decision is placed at the poem's own πᾶν τόλματον.

Source: §§IV.5, VII.3–VII.6, VIII. 

11. What the article actually establishes—and what remains conjectural
It is worth distinguishing Sharks's textual observations from the larger interpretive claims built upon them.

Claim

Evidentiary status in the article

κῆνος is distal and ὄττις is indefinite

Grammatical observation

The addressee is given voice and laughter, without visual description

Textual observation

The bodily catalogue has a particular sequence

Textual observation

The sequence represents withdrawal of the performing body

Interpretive inference

χλωρός evokes the transition from living plant to writing material

Philological and material-historical inference

The future reader occupies the man's seat

Central interpretive hypothesis

Poem 1 and poem 31 form a reciprocal circuit

Comparative literary hypothesis

The poem was deliberately designed to end at its transmitted edge

Favored, but not established

The reconstructed fifth stanza represents Sappho's actual words

Not established; explicitly illustrative

There are also three particularly important qualifications.

First: Sharks does not claim that the restored stanza proves the argument. The reading is designed to stand without it.

Second: The article acknowledges that several of its identifications are inferences. In particular, the identification of the addressee with the poetic voice and the future reader with the man are not straightforward grammatical facts.

Third: Sharks explicitly identifies conditions that could falsify his interpretation. For example, evidence that the non-jealous erotic reading independently explains the man's prominence, the catalogue's order, the colour, and the agentless dare would undermine his argument about the unexplained residue.

These qualifications matter because the article is not simply proposing an imaginative alternative to the jealousy reading. It is trying to make a comparative argument about explanatory adequacy.

Source: §§VII.1b, VII.4, VII.5a; VIII. 

Overall assessment: what is the article's deepest argument?
I would distill the argument into five propositions:

1. Sappho anticipates her own reception. The man in the opening is the grammatical and spatial position of whoever will eventually receive her voice.

2. The beloved is also the poem. The addressee's exclusively auditory presence makes the scene one of poetic reception rather than simply interpersonal observation.

3. The speaker's collapse is a transformation. The ordered destruction of her performing faculties represents the passage from living body to written medium.

4. Reading is an act of re-embodiment. The reader supplies the body through which the poet's voice becomes present again. The relationship is erotic because it involves an exchange of bodies and the investment of substance in another.

5. The poem makes its reader responsible for its survival. The final dare is not simply about the speaker's courage. It is an invitation to the reader to take up the voice and continue the poet's existence.

The most original aspect, in my view, is not the identification of the man with a future reader considered in isolation. It is the way Sharks connects that identification to the poem's entire architecture:

The poem's proposed mechanism
Living Sappho

The composing, performing body

Withdrawal of bodily faculties

The written voice

Substance invested in the medium

Transmission through time

The future reader

Occupies the seat prepared by the poem

Reading and voicing

Sappho becomes present again

The reader becomes the body through which her voice lives

The resulting thesis is much more ambitious than saying that poetry survives its author.

The poem is itself the mechanism by which its author anticipates, constructs, and solicits the body of its future reader.

And that is why the ending matters so much: the reader is not simply the beneficiary of Sappho's immortality. The reader is asked to participate in making it happen.

The article's final gesture is therefore performative. Sharks begins with “I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho,” and ends by handing the reader the same responsibility. The argument attempts to enact the very process it attributes to Sappho.

That is the most consequential feature of v3.1: it is simultaneously an interpretation of a poem, a theory of poetic transmission, and an invitation to become part of the transmission it describes.

My judgment is that Sharks's future-reader interpretation is more intellectually interesting, but the non-jealous erotic interpretation is currently the stronger reading of the surviving Greek as a whole. I would not yet accept the future-reader thesis as the poem's primary or intended meaning.

However, I think Sharks identifies something genuinely important that the conventional readings leave underexplored.

Where I think Sharks is strongest
Three things stand out.

1. The opening's indefinite grammar.

The movement from κῆνος (“that man”) to ὄττις (“whoever”) deserves more attention than it usually receives. The man is described partly through his position relative to the woman and his activity of listening.

That makes him potentially repeatable: he need not be one identifiable individual.

I find the future-reader interpretation a persuasive exploitation of that grammatical openness, even if it doesn't prove the identification.

2. The poem's structure.

Sharks is right to insist that we shouldn't treat the bodily catalogue as a collection of interchangeable symptoms.

The progression from speech failure through sensory disruption to apparent death is artistically organized. A reading that explains only the speaker's erotic distress doesn't necessarily explain why Sappho has organized the experience in precisely this way.

3. The ending.

The agentless πᾶν τόλματον is an interesting place to locate the reader's participation. It leaves something unresolved, and Sharks's interpretation gives that openness a literary function.

I particularly like the idea that the poem doesn't merely survive its author but anticipates the activity through which it will survive.

Where I think Sharks overreaches
There are three problems I would take seriously.

1. The identification of the beloved with the poetic voice is insufficiently demonstrated.

The absence of visual description is suggestive, but not decisive. Erotic poetry frequently concentrates on voice, laughter, and the effects of looking without supplying a physical portrait.

The fact that the woman is described through auditory attributes doesn't establish that she is Sappho's own voice.

2. The χλωρός argument carries too much interpretive weight.

I find the botanical and material-history discussion fascinating. But there is a substantial distance between demonstrating that χλωρός can mean fresh or moist and demonstrating that Sappho intended an allusion to the preparation of writing material.

The latter requires more evidence than semantic possibility and an analogy with papyrus.

This is perhaps the most vulnerable link in the argument because so much of the proposed transformation from body to writing surface depends on it.

3. The interpretation risks becoming too self-confirming.

The reader is identified with the man; the beloved becomes the voice; the bodily collapse becomes textual production; the ending becomes an invitation to read.

Each move supports the next, but the chain is only as strong as its least-established identification.

There is a danger of reading every feature as evidence for a theory that has already determined what the poem must be doing.

My preferred interpretation
I would actually distinguish three levels:

Level

My preferred reading

Immediate dramatic scene

Erotic overwhelm, without requiring jealousy

Poetic architecture

A carefully constructed representation of voice, absence, and selfhood

Historical and literary significance

The poem's capacity to anticipate its future readers and survive through them

This allows us to recognize something that I think Sharks gets right without requiring every detail of his argument to be true.

In particular, I would distinguish between two propositions:

Sappho deliberately wrote the man as a future reader.

Sappho wrote a poem whose structure allows future readers to occupy the man's position.

I find the second considerably more convincing.

It is also arguably more interesting. A poem need not encode a complete theory of its future reception to possess a structure that makes that reception possible.

My final verdict
Strongest

Most

reading

I would not dismiss Sharks's reading as ingenious overinterpretation. It asks an important question that conventional interpretations often neglect: What if Sappho is not merely describing the experience of losing herself, but deliberately composing the means by which she will become present to someone who has not yet been born?

That question seems to me to open a genuinely productive way of reading Fragment 31.

But I would want to see the future-reader hypothesis established more independently of the χλωρός argument and the identification of the beloved with the voice before treating it as the poem's controlling meaning.

This matters because the poem supplies its own causal relationship: looking at the beloved produces the bodily response.

The jealousy interpretation needs the man to be the cause of the speaker's distress, but the speaker's own explanation points to her encounter with the woman.

The non-jealous erotic reading therefore has a straightforward advantage: it takes the stated cause seriously rather than making the man the indispensable psychological explanation.

2. The poem's emotional climax is directed toward the woman
The opening man is described as fortunate, almost godlike. But the speaker's subsequent experience is organized around looking at the woman.

The sequence moves from the man's apparent happiness to the speaker's inability to speak, bodily disturbance, and near-death.

The beloved is the sustained focus of the speaker's experience. The man establishes a contrast, but the poem does not tell us that she wants to occupy his position or that she resents him.

A non-jealous reading preserves the erotic asymmetry: the woman is the object of overwhelming desire, while the man provides a foil for the speaker's own inability to approach or respond.

3. The comparison with the gods is rhetorical, not necessarily psychological
The man is described as equal to the gods because he can sit opposite the beloved and listen to her sweet voice.

That is an extravagant description of an apparently ordinary privilege.

The non-jealous interpretation can understand this as a measure of the beloved's erotic power: proximity to her, and access to her voice, seem almost divine.

The speaker's reaction is then intelligible without requiring resentment. She recognizes how extraordinary the experience of being near this woman must be, and discovers that she herself cannot endure it.

4. The bodily catalogue is an account of erotic experience
The non-jealous reading also has a positive explanation for the poem's physical detail.

The sequence of speechlessness, fire, impaired sight, ringing ears, sweating, trembling, and near-death gives bodily form to overwhelming desire.

Its rhetorical achievement is to make an inward emotional state progressively visible through the body.

It does not need to explain each symptom as a discrete stage of textual production. The sequence can be an intensification of erotic experience, moving from the failure of speech toward the apparent dissolution of the self.

That is a substantial poetic explanation, not merely a default interpretation.

5. The ending can resolve the erotic experience without introducing a future reader
The final πᾶν τόλματον can be understood as a return from the extremity of the experience to a general statement about endurance.

The speaker has approached the limits of what she can bear. The final assertion recognizes that one must endure what happens.

This interpretation does not require the reader to become the agent of an invitation. It reads the ending as belonging to the speaker's experience.

That is economical, although it does not exhaust the possibilities of the agentless construction.

So why do I still find Sharks's reading compelling?
Because these explanations don't settle everything.

The non-jealous erotic interpretation explains why the speaker suffers, what triggers the suffering, and how the bodily catalogue works rhetorically.

But it does not necessarily explain why the poem begins by giving such prominence to the listening man, why the opening uses the indefinite ὄττις, or why the ending takes the particular form it does.

Sharks offers a larger account of those features.

My actual disagreement with Sharks is therefore not that his reading fails to explain the erotic scene. It is that I am not convinced the additional literary architecture he proposes is sufficiently established by the Greek.

And I should acknowledge something else: my previous answer treated explanatory economy as an advantage without adequately considering that a more ambitious interpretation might explain features that the economical one leaves unexplained.

My revised position: The non-jealous erotic reading is the better-supported account of the poem's immediate meaning. Sharks offers a potentially superior account of its literary architecture, but has not, in my judgment, demonstrated that architecture conclusively.

Those are different judgments, and I should have distinguished them rather than presenting one as an uncomplicated winner.

It offers a more comprehensive account of the poem as a deliberately constructed literary object. It connects the opening's indefinite listener, the voice, the bodily dissolution, χλωροτέρα, and the ending into a coherent interpretation of poetic survival and future readership.

The non-jealous erotic reading explains the immediate emotional drama, but Sharks explains more of what makes this particular poem distinctive.
